rows: Seasonal influenza is a viral infection affecting the lungs and airways.
Influenza activity is monitored through national surveillance.
Vaccination is a principal preventive measure for eligible groups.
Diagnosis and management depend on clinical and epidemiological context.
Antiviral treatment or prophylaxis may be recommended for eligible people.
Outbreak control in closed settings requires prompt assessment and communication.
Respiratory hygiene and reducing contact while unwell can reduce transmission.
Guidance should reflect current circulating viruses, vaccine programme and antiviral resistance.
Influenza-like symptoms or a regional activity level does not prove influenza in an individual.
Individual and outbreak conclusions require symptoms, timing, testing, setting, vaccination and current surveillance evidence.
Antimicrobial resistance reduces the effectiveness of medicines used against infections.
Surveillance is central to identifying resistance threats and trends.
Laboratory characterisation and pathogen genomics can support threat detection.
Antimicrobial stewardship aims to reduce unnecessary or inappropriate use.
Infection prevention and control reduce opportunities for resistant organisms to spread.
Unusual resistance can trigger specialist assessment and outbreak support.
Data analysis and modelling help evaluate interventions.
AMR action requires coordinated human, animal and environmental measures.
A resistant laboratory result or prescribing statistic does not by itself establish an outbreak or cause.
Conclusions require organism, specimen, susceptibility, patient, setting, transmission and surveillance context.
Food manufacturers should use a food-safety management system based on HACCP principles where required.
The system should identify biological, chemical and physical hazards.
Controls should be selected for significant hazards at each process step.
Critical limits or other measurable controls should be defined where applicable.
Monitoring should show whether controls remain within the required limits.
Corrective actions should be specified for loss of control.
Verification and review should confirm that the system works.
Records should be proportionate and sufficient to demonstrate implementation.
A completed HACCP template does not prove that controls are implemented effectively.
Product conclusions require current process, hazard analysis, limits, monitoring, corrective action, verification and records.
Food incidents include actual or suspected threats to food or feed safety, quality or integrity.
Food businesses should identify and report significant incidents through the appropriate route.
Unsafe products may need withdrawal from the supply chain.
A recall may be required where products have reached consumers.
Traceability information supports identification of affected products and customers.
Incident management should preserve an auditable record of decisions and evidence.
Authorities and businesses may need coordinated risk communication.
Root-cause and corrective-action review can help prevent recurrence.
A complaint or test result does not automatically define the scale or cause of a food incident.
Incident conclusions require product, batch, hazard, distribution, test, traceability, exposure and authority evidence.
